units.title: Unit 11 — Working life
learningObjectives: Describe employment arrangements, career transitions and the income people earn using natural verb–noun combinations.
Use collocations for professional roles, job changes, promotions and offers with appropriate register.
Explain work-life priorities, workload and resignation decisions through established idiomatic expressions.
Avoid the common verb and preposition errors associated with work, pressure, job-sharing and career advancement.

items.pt: entrar para a equipe; integrar o quadro de funcionários
items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: After a successful interview, Nadia will join the staff next month.
items.note: Join the staff describes becoming an employee of a particular organisation.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: All members of staff must complete the safety course.
items.note: Especially common in British English when referring collectively to employees.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: It is difficult to make a living from occasional translation work.
items.note: Make a living refers to earning enough money to support oneself.

items.pt: ganhar bem; ter boa renda para viver
items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: Experienced interpreters can earn a good living by working remotely.
items.note: Earn a good living stresses a comfortably adequate income from work.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: The most rewarding aspects of the job involve solving real problems.
items.note: Aspect of the job is a natural phrase for an individual feature of employment.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: Our project manager will go on maternity leave in December.
items.note: Go on maternity leave is the usual expression for beginning the period away from work.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: She returned from maternity leave to find her department had grown.
items.note: Return from maternity leave refers to resuming work after the leave ends.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: After the move, Paulo decided to go part-time for six months.
items.note: Go part-time describes changing from full-time to fewer working hours.

items.pt: dividir uma vaga de trabalho com outra pessoa
items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: Two researchers agreed to do a job-share while raising young children.
items.note: A job-share is one full-time position divided between two employees.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: The company went through a difficult period after losing its main client.
items.note: Go through expresses experiencing a challenging period; the particle through remains.

items.pt: demitir funcionários por corte de postos de trabalho
items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: The manufacturer may lay off staff if orders continue to fall.
items.note: Lay off commonly indicates redundancy caused by insufficient work, not individual misconduct.

items.pt: tornar-se profissional autônomo; trabalhar como freelancer
items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: After ten years at the agency, Malik decided to go freelance.
items.note: Go freelance means stop being a regular employee and offer services independently.

items.word: build up a network of contacts
items.pt: construir uma rede de contatos profissionais
items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: Attending conferences helped her build up a network of contacts.
items.note: Build up suggests developing a network gradually over time.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: The consultancy handled a substantial volume of work during the audit.
items.note: Substantial modifies volume to stress a large quantity of tasks.

items.section: A · Working arrangements and career transitions
items.example: We faced a ridiculous volume of work before the product launch.
items.note: Informal intensification of volume of work; often implies the amount is excessive.

items.example: Dr Rahman hopes to practise medicine in a rural hospital.
items.note: Practise medicine is the standard British English phrase for working as a doctor.

items.pt: encontrar e consolidar um nicho profissional para si
items.example: She carved a niche for herself as a specialist in accessible design.
items.note: Carve a niche for yourself means develop a distinctive role or area of expertise.

items.example: After a decade in management, he was ready for fresh challenges.
items.note: Fresh challenges refers to new demands that offer stimulation or development.

items.pt: trocar temporariamente de função com outro profissional
items.example: Two engineers plan to do a job swap between the regional offices.
items.note: Job swap differs from job-share: workers exchange posts rather than split one.

items.pt: seu colega de função equivalente em outra equipe ou organização
items.example: The finance director spoke to her opposite number at the partner firm.
items.note: An opposite number holds a corresponding position elsewhere, not an opposing opinion.

items.example: Amelia will take up a post at the university in September.
items.note: Formal combination meaning begin working in a new position.

items.example: He held a senior position in the laboratory for six years.
items.note: Hold a position describes occupying a job or office, often over an extended period.

items.example: Although she likes her current role, she remains open to offers.
items.note: Open to offers indicates willingness to consider other employment opportunities.

items.example: The candidate received a tempting offer from a start-up.
items.note: Tempting collocates with offer when it is attractive and hard to refuse.

items.example: Before applying abroad, I need to put together a CV in English.
items.note: Put together means compile information into a coherent document.

items.example: Recent graduates often apply for jobs in several different cities.
items.note: Apply for a job takes for, not to; apply to a company uses a different complement.

items.pt: um programa de progressão acelerada na carreira
items.example: The company introduced a fast-track scheme for promising trainees.
items.note: Fast-track describes accelerated training or advancement, not literal transport.

items.pt: subir na carreira; progredir na hierarquia
items.example: She moved up the ladder after repeatedly leading successful projects.
items.note: Figurative career phrase for earning promotions to more senior posts.

items.pt: uma mudança de opinião ou decisão
items.example: I was going to accept the transfer, but I had a change of heart.
items.note: A change of heart is a revision of feeling or intention, often reversing a plan.

items.example: During a demanding project, it is important to get your priorities right.
items.note: This fixed phrase means decide what deserves the most attention.

items.example: Patient safety must take priority over cost reductions.
items.note: Take priority over establishes that one concern is more important than another.

items.pt: pedir demissão formalmente; entregar a carta de demissão
items.example: He handed in his resignation after accepting a role overseas.
items.note: Hand in your resignation is the conventional phrase for formally resigning.

items.example: The inspection team was under considerable pressure to finish by Friday.
items.note: Say under considerable pressure or under a lot of pressure, not under high pressure.

items.example: New managers can be under a lot of pressure during restructuring.
items.note: A common alternative to under considerable pressure; high pressure is atypical here.

items.example: The interns do important work for the outreach programme.
items.note: The normal verb is do work; make work usually means create additional tasks.

items.pt: dar trabalho a alguém; criar tarefas adicionais para alguém
items.example: The poorly designed form made work for the administration team.
items.note: Unlike do work, make work for someone means generate extra work for that person.

items.pt: distribuir um relatório entre as pessoas envolvidas
items.example: Please circulate the report to the committee before the meeting.
items.note: Circulate a report means send it around to a group for reading or action.

items.example: My colleague holds a similar position at another research centre.
items.note: Hold can combine with position to describe a continuing job role.

units.title: Unit 12 — New employment
learningObjectives: Discuss shortlisting, references, job requirements and the capabilities expected of new employees.
Distinguish formal descriptions of workplace misconduct and dismissal from informal workplace expressions.
Describe workload, employment conditions, staff turnover and potential career progression accurately.
Use natural collocations for labour action, pay, overtime and professional responsibility without register mistakes.

items.example: Your experience seems to fit the job description extremely well.
items.note: Fit the job description means match the skills and duties specified in an advert.

items.example: Choosing one finalist from fifty strong candidates is a daunting task.
items.note: Daunting suggests a task feels difficult enough to discourage or intimidate.

items.pt: reduzir a lista de opções ou candidatos
items.example: The panel must narrow the list down before the final interviews.
items.note: Narrow down a list is a standard phrasal-verb pattern for reducing choices.

items.example: Before making an offer, the employer will take up references.
items.note: Particularly British and fairly formal recruitment language for contacting referees.

items.example: The developers need to work as a team to meet the deadline.
items.note: Work as a team describes close cooperation towards a shared goal.

items.example: Apprentices are expected to master new skills throughout the course.
items.note: Master skills means acquire a high level of competence, not merely try them.

items.example: Junior staff can take on responsibility gradually with proper support.
items.note: Take on responsibility means accept accountability for tasks or decisions.

items.example: Union members voted to take industrial action over unsafe conditions.
items.note: Industrial action includes organised worker protest, potentially including strikes.

items.example: The workers threatened to stage a strike if negotiations failed.
items.note: Stage or go on a strike is idiomatic; make a strike is not.

items.example: Bus drivers may go on strike unless an agreement is reached.
items.note: Go on strike is the usual phrase for workers stopping work collectively.

items.pt: conduta profissional inadequada; infração ética no exercício da profissão
items.example: The regulator opened an investigation into professional misconduct.
items.note: Formal term for behaviour that breaches professional standards.

items.example: The supervisor was relieved of his duties pending an internal inquiry.
items.note: Formal wording for removal from a role; it may or may not mean permanent dismissal.

items.example: The director left the company under mysterious circumstances.
items.note: Under mysterious circumstances presents the surrounding events as unexplained.

items.pt: demitido injustamente ou de forma ilegal
items.example: The tribunal concluded that the technician had been wrongfully dismissed.
items.note: A formal, often legal expression for a dismissal that violates rights.

items.pt: defender alguém; posicionar-se a favor de alguém
items.example: She stood up for a colleague who had been treated unfairly.
items.note: Stand up for means support or defend someone against criticism or unfair treatment.

items.example: It takes strength of character to challenge an unfair decision.
items.note: A fixed noun phrase for moral courage and firmness in difficult situations.

items.example: Independent traders feared they would lose their livelihood after the closure.
items.note: Livelihood refers to how you earn a living, not merely your current title.

items.example: Can we pencil in a meeting for Thursday and confirm it later?
items.note: Pencil in means make a tentative arrangement, subject to later confirmation.

items.pt: organizar e esvaziar sua mesa de trabalho
items.example: I need to clear my desk before the office renovation.
items.note: May mean tidy the workspace, or pack belongings when leaving a job.

items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: After months of applications, Leila finally landed a new job.
items.note: Informal verb land means secure a position, often after an effort.

items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The nurses reported a heavy workload during the winter surge.
items.note: Heavy workload is the natural adjective–noun combination for many demanding duties.

items.pt: trabalhar em horários pouco convencionais ou inconvenientes
items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: Hospital staff often work unsocial hours, including nights and weekends.
items.note: Common British English phrase for shifts outside ordinary social or business hours.

items.pt: tarefas braçais ou rotineiras de baixo prestígio
items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The assistant disliked spending every afternoon on menial tasks.
items.note: Menial describes low-status routine work, sometimes considered beneath a worker’s skills.

items.pt: fazer tarefas externas ou pequenos serviços
items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The office assistant often has to run errands across town.
items.note: Run errands means do practical short tasks such as collecting documents or supplies.

items.pt: um salário suficiente para cobrir as necessidades básicas
items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The campaign demanded a living wage for all contracted cleaners.
items.note: A living wage aims to meet essential living costs; it is not necessarily the legal minimum.

items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: Employees complained about unpaid overtime before the product release.
items.note: Unpaid overtime means working beyond contracted hours without extra compensation.

items.pt: faltar ao trabalho fingindo estar doente
items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: He joked about throwing a sickie to watch the final at home.
items.note: Very informal British English; implies claiming illness when not actually sick.

items.pt: ser mandado embora; levar uma demissão
items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: He could get the sack if he repeatedly ignores safety procedures.
items.note: Informal British English for being dismissed by an employer.

items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The graduate accepted the role because it offered good prospects.
items.note: Prospects refers to future opportunities, especially promotion and career development.

items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The investigation revealed the use of sweated labour in small workshops.
items.note: A critical term for workers paid very little in poor conditions.

items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The mentoring programme helps employees realise their potential.
items.note: Realise your potential means develop and achieve the abilities you possess.

items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: A high turnover of staff can disrupt customer service.
items.note: Turnover of staff measures how frequently workers leave and are replaced.

items.pt: perseverar até o fim; não desistir do caminho escolhido
items.section: B · Working conditions and career prospects
items.example: The trainee struggled at first but stayed the course and qualified.
items.note: Figurative phrase for continuing despite difficulty until the goal is reached.

items.example: Promotion gave him the chance to take on more responsibility.
items.note: More responsibility extends the same productive take on pattern.

items.word: be capable of mastering new skills
items.pt: ser capaz de dominar novas habilidades
items.example: The new recruits are capable of mastering new skills quickly.
items.note: Capable of is followed by an -ing form, here mastering, not a bare infinitive.

items.example: She feared she might lose her job after the department closed.
items.note: A neutral phrase for becoming unemployed; lose your livelihood is broader.

items.example: Workers who believe they were unfairly dismissed can seek advice.
items.note: More general wording than wrongfully dismissed, which can have a legal nuance.

items.example: I sometimes do overtime when our team is preparing a release.
items.note: Overtime commonly combines with do or work; doing overtime does not imply payment.

items.example: Some employees get paid overtime, while others receive time off.
items.note: Paid overtime contrasts with unpaid overtime; get paid emphasises compensation.
